description: Tidy tables describing trial-level behavioral data for cognitive tests and questionnaires, derived from raw events. The component, parameter, and score tables are keyed by their natural keys and carry no surrogate primary key.

tables.name: StudyflowLog
tables.label: StudyflowLog
tables.description: The run log: one row per activity run — a single execution of one activity by one agent, with restarts counted as separate runs. Shipped as `studyflow_log.csv` in the agent's folder. This is the *realized* record of what an agent actually did; it is not the study-level plan (the BPMN studyflow diagram authored in the `studyflow` schema family), which describes what was designed to happen.
notes: This table is what makes an activity run addressable: every other trial table carries its `runtime_id`, so files can be concatenated across agents, sessions, and attempts without losing scope.
A run that was started and abandoned before any trial finished produces no rows in the other tables; its row here is the only record that it happened.
Selecting the last complete attempt is a filter plus a join: keep rows with `status` = `completed`, take the largest `attempt` per (`agent_id`, `instrument_id`), then join `Response` on `runtime_id`.
The same run is identified in the event layer by `bdm:runtime_id`, so events and trials join directly.

fields.name: runtime_id
fields.description: Primary key: a dataset-wide unique identifier for this activity run. A UUID is recommended so that runs stay distinguishable when datasets are pooled. Equals the event layer's `bdm:runtime_id` for the same run.

fields.name: agent_id
fields.description: The agent who performed this run. Resolves in the `Agent` table of the `agents` family, shipped as `agents.csv` at the dataset root.

fields.name: session_index
fields.description: The 1-based session, within this agent, that the run belongs to.

fields.name: session_uuid
fields.description: Globally unique identifier (UUID, RFC 9562) of the session, when one was assigned. Matches `session_uuid` in the `Response` table.

fields.name: activity_index
fields.description: The 1-based order of this activity within the session.
fields.range: 1-based index of activity within the session

fields.name: instrument_id
fields.description: The instrument (task) that ran.

fields.name: timeline_id
fields.description: The specific parameterization of the instrument that ran.

fields.name: attempt
fields.description: The 1-based ordinal of this run of the activity within the session: the first run has `attempt` = 1, a restart after an interruption has `attempt` = 2, and so on. This is what identifies sessions that were interrupted and possibly restarted several times.
fields.range: 1-based index of the run within (agent, session, activity)

fields.name: instrument_repetition
fields.description: The number of times this instrument had already been completed by this agent earlier in the study (0 the first time). Counts one agent's own history across sessions — not completions across participants, and not restarts within a session (that is `attempt`).

fields.name: timeline_repetition
fields.description: The same count for this timeline: how many times this agent had already completed it earlier in the study.

fields.name: status
fields.description: How far this run got: `initialized`, `in_progress`, `completed`, or `abandoned`. Derived from the lifecycle events where an event stream exists, and authored directly otherwise. This is the authoritative record of completion; `Response.status` is a copy of it.

values.description: The run was created but no content was ever shown to the agent (no `bdm:started`).
The run started but has no terminal state — still running, or interrupted without a recorded ending (e.g. an engine crash).
All required content was done (`bdm:completed`).
The run ended without completion (`bdm:abandoned`); see `abandon_reason`.

fields.name: abandon_reason
fields.description: Why the run ended without completion, when known (e.g. `timeout`, `withdrew`, `technical_failure`). Mirrors the event layer's `bdm:abandon_reason`. Empty unless `status` is `abandoned`.

fields.name: start_datetime
fields.description: When the run started — the moment the first content was shown to the agent (the event layer's `bdm:started`).

fields.name: end_datetime
fields.description: When the run reached its terminal state, whether completed or abandoned.

fields.name: anchor_datetime
fields.description: The datetime (RFC 9557, with timezone offset) corresponding to zero on this run's monotonic clock — the bridge from engine seconds to wall-clock time. It belongs to the run rather than the session because a restart starts a new engine clock. Datetime columns in the trial tables are derived through it.
notes: See the `engine_seconds` and `anchor_datetime` terms in the Behaverse vocabulary.

tables.name: Response
tables.label: Response
tables.description: Main table where each row describes a response in a trial.

fields.name: runtime_id
fields.description: Identifies the activity run (one specific execution of an activity by one agent, distinguishing restarts) this response belongs to. Unique dataset-wide, so rows from different agents, sessions, or attempts stay distinguishable when files are concatenated. Resolves in the `StudyflowLog` table, and equals the event layer's `bdm:runtime_id` for the same run.

fields.name: response_id
fields.description: A unique identifier assigned to responses in temporal order, meaning that larger IDs correspond to more recent responses that occurred later in time. This ID is unique within one activity run; the dataset-wide key is the pair (`runtime_id`, `response_id`).
notes: This identifier is used by other tables, for example `Stimulus` table which describes in greater detail the sequence of images shown during a trial, their timing, and visual properties. That table will refer to this `id` in order to link those descriptions (typically multiple lines in the Stimulus table) to a unique row in the `Response` table.

fields.name: study_name
fields.description: The name of the study or experiment.

fields.name: group_name
fields.description: Agents may be assigned to different groups. Typically, different groups will have different experiences within a study.

fields.name: agent_id
fields.description: A unique identifier assigned to the agent (typically person) generating the responses. This ID tracks their participation and responses throughout the study. Resolves in the `Agent` table of the `agents` family, shipped as `agents.csv` at the dataset root.

fields.name: session_index
fields.description: When there are multiple sessions, this variable indicates the order of each session (i.e., the first session completed by the agent has `session_index` = 1, the second session has `session_index` = 2; even if the second session is an exact repetition of the first one).
notes: We currently don’t use session_name and session_repetition in this table.

fields.name: session_uuid
fields.description: A globally unique identifier (UUID) for the session, assigned by the recording engine when the session starts. Unlike `session_index` (a per-agent ordinal), `session_uuid` identifies the session across datasets and systems; it is the value event streams refer to when scoping events to a session.
notes: Optional: datasets recorded before this field existed have no value to backfill. New recording engines should always populate it.

fields.name: activity_index
fields.description: When agents complete multiple activities (e.g., a cognitive test followed by a questionnaire), this variable indicates the order of each activity (i.e., the first activity completed by the agent has `activity_index` = 1, the second activity has `activity_index` = 2; even if the second activity is an exact repetition of the first one).
fields.range: 1-based index of activity within the agent-level data
notes: See `StudyflowLog` table for more details.

fields.name: response_index
fields.description: The 1-based ordinal position of this response within the agent's participation in the study. response_index is nested within agents — not within any lower-level construct (session, activity, block, or trial) — so the counter starts at the agent's first response and increments to their last without ever resetting. Its maximum value for a given agent equals the number of responses recorded from that agent in the study.
fields.range: 1-based integer, nested within agent (never reset across sessions or activities)
notes: Often redundant with `episode_index`, but not always: in multitask settings an agent may emit two distinct responses at (approximately) the same time; each response gets its own `response_index`, but both share one `episode_index` value.

In a questionnaire where agents may answer questions in any order, stimulus_index encodes the order of the questions on the page while response_index encodes the order in which the agent answered them.
Not to be confused with response_option_index (which option was chosen) or response_id (an identifier unique within this table, assigned in temporal order).

fields.name: language
fields.description: The language the task was completed in, expressed as a two-letter code within the [ISO_639-1 standard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_ISO_639-1_codes).

fields.name: instrument_id
fields.description: The unique identifier of the instrument used for collecting data (e.g., the name of the computer script used to run the test). Unique in the `Instrument` table and corresponding files in the `instruments/` folder.

fields.name: instrument_repetition
fields.description: The number of times this particular instrument has already been completed **by this agent** anywhere earlier in this study. It counts one agent's own history across sessions — never how many times the instrument was completed across participants. This variable has a value 0 the first time an instrument is used.
notes: Distinct from `attempt`, which counts runs of the activity within the current session and is what identifies a session that was interrupted and restarted. See the `StudyflowLog` table.

fields.name: attempt
fields.description: The 1-based ordinal of this activity run within the session: the first run of the activity has `attempt` = 1, a restart after an interruption has `attempt` = 2, and so on. This is what distinguishes several runs of the same activity that now live in one file together.
fields.range: 1-based index of the run within (agent, session, activity); see `attempt` in the `StudyflowLog` table

fields.name: status
fields.description: How far this response's activity run got — copied from the run's row in the `StudyflowLog` table so that trials from abandoned runs can be filtered without a join. The `StudyflowLog` table is authoritative; a disagreement between the two is a dataset error.

values.description: The run was created but no content was ever shown to the agent (no `bdm:started`).
The run started but has no terminal state — still running, or interrupted without a recorded ending (e.g. an engine crash).
All required content was done (`bdm:completed`).
The run ended without completion (`bdm:abandoned`); see `abandon_reason`.

notes: Derived, and only final once the run has ended; runs recorded while still in flight read `in_progress`. In a published dataset every run has reached a terminal state.

fields.name: timeline_id
fields.description: Timelines are specific parameterization of an instrument and their identifiers are unique within the corresponding table for the instrument in the `instruments/` folder.

fields.name: timeline_repetition
fields.description: The number of times this particular timeline has already been completed anytime in the past by this particular agent in this study. This variable has a value 0 the first time a timeline is completed.

fields.name: multitask_type
fields.description: Agents may be required to perform multiple tasks at the same time. This variable indicates the type of multitasking required.

values.description: There are two independent tasks that need to be completed in parallel.
The task requires multiple successive stages or involves tasks that are dependent/coupled.

notes: If no multitasking was involved, leave this field blank.
This characterization of `multitask_type` is rudimentary and will likely evolve in the future.

fields.name: task_index
fields.description: When `multitask_type` is not empty, `task_index` refers to each of the individual tasks. For example, for auditory-visual dual N-back, `task_index=1` is the auditory task and `task_index=2` is the visual task.

fields.name: subtrial_count
fields.description: The number of subtrials (successive dependent stages, each with its own stimulus → response → outcome cycle) that make up this trial; equals the largest `subtrial_index` among this trial's rows in the `Subtrial` table. Derived; 1 for simple single-stage trials.
notes: Not the same as `response_count`, which counts the pieces of a single response: a digit-span trial recalling "3-5-7" has `response_count` = 3 but `subtrial_count` = 1 (one stimulus, one recall, one evaluation), while a two-step trial has `subtrial_count` = 2 (two stages, each with its own stimulus and outcome).

fields.name: job_type
fields.description: The general type of operation the agent needs to perform. The job typically is expressed as a verb (e.g., "recall", "sort") and can be the same for different instruments (e.g., Digit Span test and Spatial Span test both have a job of type "recall-forward").

fields.name: job_description
fields.description: The more specific description of a job, which gives more information about what the participant sees and has to do. Whereas the `job_type` typically uses only verbs and adjectives, the `job_description` also contains nouns (e.g., “recall-digits-forward”, “recall-letters-backward”).

fields.name: job_repeat
fields.description: Whether this trial's job has not been seen before in this timeline (i.e., specific version of the instrument).

values.description: The job has never been seen before by this agent in the current study.
The job is the same as the previous trial.
The job is different from the previous trial but has been seen prior in the timeline.

fields.name: block_index
fields.description: Refers to the order in which this block has been experienced by the agent. When there are multiple blocks, this variable indicates the order of each block (i.e., the first block completed by the agent has `block_index=1`, the second block has `block_index=2`, even if the second block is an exact repetition of the first one).
fields.range: 1-based index of the block within the timeline
notes: In questionnaires, `block_index` may refer to distinct pages where each page may contain multiple questions.

fields.name: block_name
fields.description: The name of a particular block in a timeline. If the same block is completed twice in a row, they would have different `block_index` values (1 and 2, respectively) but they would have the same `block_name` (e.g., “NB_timeline1_block1”). More details about the `block_name` is available in the `Instrument` table.

fields.name: block_type
fields.description: Specifies the experimental role of the block (e.g., tutorial, practice, test, instruction).

values.description: A simplified version of the test designed to teach agents how the test works.
Typically identical to the main test blocks, but used to get agents accustomed to the task in a no-stakes environment.
Primary blocks used to measure the desired behaviors.
Presents written and/or visual instructions to the agent.

fields.name: transformation_name
fields.description: Refers to the specific events-to-trials function used to construct rows of this table from raw events. The transformation (or projection in DDD terminology) embodies the definition of a trial for a particular task. The transformer name refers to a code in the format of a function `f(trial_state, event) => trial_state`, where `event` is the event occurred during the performance of the task, and `trial_state` is the data stored for the trial. The final state of a trial is thus the result of applying a sequence of projections such that `trial = f(f(f(initial()), e), e), e)`.
notes: - The transformation/projection encapsulates the domain rules that define a "trial" for a given task. It defines what constitutes a "trial".

fields.name: trial_index
fields.description: Sequential identifier representing number of times transformation rule to the events occurred. It increases with each re-computation of the trial based on updated or newly received events.
notes: This field emphasizes order of trials and alignment with projection-based definition of trials. A more complete name would be `projection_index` or `projected_trial_index`. For brevity, BDM uses `trial_index` instead.

fields.name: episode_index
fields.description: Episodes are temporally distinct bins of time (no overlap and discrete). The binning of the time into successive episodes depends on the task; it is mostly used and necessary to group data in cases where two distinct trials occurred at the same time (e.g., dual N-back).

fields.name: trial_start_datetime
fields.description: The datetime at which the first event of the trial occurred.

fields.name: trial_seed
fields.description: Random seed used in the trial (if any).

fields.name: stimulus_index
fields.description: Indexes in chronological (or spatial) order the stimuli shown within an instrument (counting one stimulus per response). `stimulus_index` may for instance be used to refer to the nth question asked within a questionnaire.
notes: Use semicolon-separated indices if more than one stimulus was presented, e.g., `1;2;3`.
In a questionnaire this is the position of the question: `stimulus_index` = 1 is the first question presented, = 23 the twenty-third.

fields.name: stimulus_id
fields.description: Is a unique identifier for the (unitary, set or sequence of) stimuli presented during a trial; if those exact same stimuli are repeated in a different trial, that trial would have the same value for stimulus_id. stimulus_id may also be used to refer to a specific message or question in a questionnaire.
fields.range: `stimulus_id` in the `Stimulus` table, within the same `runtime_id`

fields.name: stimulus_type
fields.description: The kind of stimulus shown; BDM distinguishes messages and questions.

values.description: The stimulus is a message shown to agents (e.g., task instructions).
The stimulus may consist of text, images, and/or sounds; it requires agents to make a decision based on the content of the stimulus.

fields.name: stimulus_onset
fields.description: Duration between the start of the trial and the appearance of the stimulus, in seconds.
notes: In questionnaires this is typically 0, since the question is usually present from the start of the trial.

fields.name: stimulus_panel_count
fields.description: The number of panels or screen areas stimuli may appear on during the trial. For example, in a task where stimuli to be compared are presented on the left and right side of the screen, stimulus_panel_count = 2.

fields.name: stimulus_structure
fields.description: The structure of the stimuli shown during the trial.

values.description: Only one stimulus is shown, alone.
Many stimuli are shown, either at the same time or not; order does not matter.
Multiple stimuli are shown, either at the same time or not; order does matter (order may be indicated by the order of presentation or by a digit, for example).

fields.name: stimulus_structure_source_type
fields.description: Indicates the type of method used to generate the `stimulus_structure` (relevant when a trial displays a set or sequence of stimuli).

values.description: No structure to generate: `stimulus_structure` is `unitary`.
The structure of stimuli is hard-coded in a file.
A procedure was used to generate the stimulus structure.

fields.name: stimulus_structure_source
fields.description: Refers to the specific generator used to produce the stimulus_structure (e.g., sequence of digits in a digit span test). When no generator was used, this variable has a value of none.

fields.name: stimulus_set_size
fields.description: The number of different values each presented stimulus could have taken. This value gives an indication of the complexity of the stimulus space. When this number is large we set this variable to infinity, when for any reason it was not computed, it has a value of NA.
notes: To specify "infinity" in a CSV file we use +Inf and -Inf; these are correctly recognized in R (tidyverse) and Python (pandas) as being valid numbers rather than strings.

fields.name: stimulus_count
fields.description: The number of stimuli shown to the participant during the trial.
fields.range: matches the number of stimuli in `stimulus_id`

fields.name: stimulus_source_type
fields.description: A stimulus is typically created using a particular procedure/algorithm ("generator") or is sampled from a particular set ("set"). This variable indicates which of these two applies for the current stimulus.

values.description: Sampled from a fixed set.
Created using a procedure/algorithm.

fields.name: stimulus_source
fields.description: Refers to the specific generator or set the stimulus belongs to. Stimuli that stem from the same source have the same data scheme and could thus be described in a table named after stimulus_source (i.e., stimulus_source indicates which table contains the full information about the stimulus; e.g., "digit1to9").

fields.name: stimulus_index_in_source
fields.description: Index of the stimulus within the table referred to by stimulus_source. : For example, if stimulus_source == "digit1to9", stimulus_index_in_source = 1 refers to "1" while for stimulus_source == "LettersAtoD", stimulus_index_in_source = 1 refers to "A".
notes: It is not because a particular stimulus_source is used in a given timeline that all possible stimuli of that source are displayed to the user. For example, the AX-CPT may use "upper-case-letters" but only use a subset of those letters (e.g., "A", "B", "X", "Y"). Whenever possible, we specify the most relevant/specific set (e.g., "digit1to9" rather than "digit").

fields.name: stimulus_position_index
fields.description: Refers to discrete positions on the screen the stimulus may appear on. The set and ordering of possible positions depends on the test. Whenever possible, it follows a natural order (left to right, top to bottom), but in free-form layouts, indices are arbitrary.

fields.name: stimulus_description
fields.description: A human readable, compact description of the main aspects of the stimulus. The description for a given stimulus depends on the task but follows a specific template for a given task. Because of this, it looks like the stimulus_description could be "parsed" and "tidied"---however, this is not the intention; parsed/tidied data will be available in other tables; description is for human readability and facilitates the understanding of the data.
notes: In some cases, when stimuli are too complex or can't be precisely described, a summary of all stimuli is given instead.

For questionnaires this holds the question text as presented, in English. When a question was shown in another language (recorded in `language`), the translations belong in the questionnaire's supplementary resources rather than in this column.

fields.name: stimulus_role
fields.description: The role the stimulus plays within the trial.

values.description: A stimulus the agent must process and which should trigger the completion of the response (e.g., classify, reach, memorize) if the agent is doing the task as intended. In some cases (e.g., in a go/no-go task) the correct response to a stimulus is to *not* click the button; the stimulus that triggered the decision not to click the button is still a *target*.
A stimulus the agent must process but which does not trigger the completion of the response (e.g., the first two stimuli in a 2-back test).
A stimulus the agent should not process at all (i.e., ignore) and which is unrelated to the correct execution of the task.
A stimulus giving spatial location information that agents could use to improve their performance.
A stimulus specifying which job the agent should perform.
A stimulus signaling the agent that they should abort the current action.
A stimulus indicating which stimulus to respond about.

fields.name: option_source_type
fields.description: A set of options is typically created using a particular procedure/algorithm (“generator”) or is sampled from a particular set (“set”). This variable indicates which of these two applies for the current options.

values.description: Sampled from a fixed set.
Created using a procedure/algorithm.

fields.name: option_source
fields.description: Refers to the specific generator or set that determined the options on a given trial. Option that stem from the same source have the same data scheme and could thus be described in a table named after option_source (i.e., option_source indicates which table contains the full information about the option set).
notes: While there is a stimulus_index_in_source to refer to the particular stimulus that was used, we don’t have an equivalent option_index_in_source since all options are displayed. Instead, we use response_option_index and expected_response_option_index to refer to a particular option within the set of options.

Identifies where the option set came from (e.g. `likert_1_to_7`, `gender`). This is what lets a reader determine whether two datasets used the same scale, and it is the natural attachment point for psychometric metadata about that scale.

fields.name: option_count
fields.description: The number of options the participant can choose from on a given trial.

fields.name: option_id
fields.description: Is a unique identifier for the option (set or generator) used on a given trial.
fields.range: `option_id` in the `Option` table, within the same `runtime_id`
notes: A question is often reused with different option sets (e.g. `agreement_7` vs `agreement_5`), and the resulting measures are not interchangeable. The combination of a question and its options is what the survey literature calls an *item*; BDM has no separate identifier for it — an item is `stimulus_id` together with `option_id`.

fields.name: option_data_type
fields.description: Describes the type of data this option entails.

values.description: A set of unordered labels (e.g., “Luxembourg”, “France”, “Germany”).
Ordered values without a clear distance (e.g., “a lot”, “a bit”, “not at all”).
Ordered values with clear distances but no absolute zero (e.g., 10 versus 20 degrees Celsius).
Values with clear distance metrics and an absolute zero (e.g., length in cm).

fields.name: measurement_type
fields.description: Describes the type of measurement implied by `Option`, which in turn has implications on how that data should be processed during analysis.

values.description: A set of unordered labels (e.g., “Luxembourg”, “France”, “Germany”).
Ordered values without a clear distance (e.g., “a lot”, “a bit”, “not at all”).
Ordered values with clear distances but no absolute zero (e.g., 10 versus 20 degrees Celsius).
Values with clear distance metrics and an absolute zero (e.g., length in cm).

fields.name: input_interface_type
fields.description: Refers to the type of interface agents used to input actions.

values.description: A keyboard is displayed on the screen.
Dedicated buttons on the screen.
Stimuli serve as buttons.
A text field is displayed on the screen.
A slider is displayed on the screen.

fields.name: input_action_type
fields.description: Refers to the type of action the agent performs to give a response.
notes: The type of input_action determines the structure of detailed response data (i.e., mouse-click data is different from key-press data).

fields.name: input_count
fields.description: The number of inputs (i.e., actions) the user made during the trial.
notes: For mouse-drag, it corresponds to the number of drag points that have been sampled during the drag-and-drop.

fields.name: expected_response_option_index
fields.description: The index of the option the agent is expected to choose from the set of options.
notes: When expected_response_option_index = 0, it means that the agent should not respond at all.

Sometimes stimuli serve both as stimuli and as response options as agents have to click on a particular stimuli to give their response (e.g., spatial span, odd one out). It is convenient in those cases to use stimulus_position_index to order/index the options (i.e., option_index == stimulus_position_index) and consequently also the responses.

fields.name: expected_response_description
fields.description: A description of the expected response using the same convention as response_description.

fields.name: response_structure
fields.description: The structure of the response required by the agent.

values.description: The agent provides a single input (e.g., chooses option *same*).
The agent provides a set of information, and the order does not matter (e.g., list words that start with the letter *A*).
The agent provides a sequence of information, and the order matters (e.g., a sequence of memorized digits in their order of appearance).

notes: Note that the distinction between set and sequence refers to the importance of order information to evaluate if the response is correct or not; a response with a set structure may unfold over time (each piece of information is given in a particular temporal order) and it may be of scientific interest to take into account that order; however, the order itself is not important within the task itself. For example, in the [MOT task](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiple_object_tracking) one may ask agents to point to all dots that hide a token. If agents point to all such dots they will be correct no matter in which order the dots were clicked in.

fields.name: response_type
fields.description: The form of the response act — what kind of answer is collected: `choice`, `rating`, `ranking` (selected from what is presented) or `production`, `motor` (generated by the agent). Declared per response even where derivable from other fields, because the derivations then serve as validation checks rather than the source of truth.

values.description: Select mode: pick one (or more) of the presented options.
Select mode: place a judgment on an ordinal scale (e.g. Likert). Validation: implies options with ordinal `measurement_type`.
Select mode: order the presented items. Validation: implies `response_structure: sequence` over the option set.
Generate mode: produce the content of the answer (typed text or numbers, drawings, spoken words). Validation: typically co-occurs with `option_count` empty/null.
Generate mode: a continuous movement is itself the answer (e.g. reaching, tracing).

notes: Orthogonal to `job_type`: a value belongs in `response_type` iff it can vary while the job is held fixed *and* recur across different jobs (a *recall* job can collect production or choice; a rating can serve a *decide* or a *judge* job). "Recall" is therefore a job, never a response_type.
The coarse mode (select vs generate) is implied by the value and is not a separate column: choice/rating/ranking are selections; production/motor are generations.

fields.name: response_count
fields.description: Each trial contains by definition only one response. However, when response_structure is other than unitary, a response comprises multiple pieces of information (e.g., “3-5-7” could be one response in the digit span task and this response contains three components, namely “3”, “5” and “7”). response_count refers to the number of components that make up a response (not the number of responses within a trial).
notes: Not the same as `input_count`: an agent may in some cases change their response multiple times before submitting the final response; in such cases there are many more inputs than there are components to the final response.
While we have stimulus_set_size we currently don’t have a response_set_size, but we do have option_count and response_count.

fields.name: response_option_index
fields.description: The index of the option the participant chose, starting from 1.
notes: A value of 0 means the agent chose none of the options (e.g., a “no-go” response in a go/no-go task).
Directly comparable to `expected_response_option_index`.
Refers to an entry in the `Option` table.

Not to be confused with response_index: response_option_index indexes into the set of options (*which* option was chosen), whereas response_index is the ordinal position of the response itself within the agent's study participation (see the response_index field; cf. also response_element_index in the Input table for the pieces of one response).
Records which option the agent chose by its position in the offered set. Essential whenever options are presented in a random order, since the label alone does not identify the choice.

fields.name: response_description
fields.description: A description of participant’s response; typically the description of the option that was chosen.
notes: Directly comparable to `expected_response_description`.
For questionnaires this is typically the label of the chosen option (e.g. "strongly agree"), the text entered in a free-text field, or a numeric entry.

fields.name: response_numeric
fields.description: A numeric value associated with a particular response; this could be a numeric value entered directly by the agent or the numeric meaning of a selected option (for example, the choice of option "Never" may be associated with the numeric value of 0). Note that this variable describes the agent's response; it does not describe the value (e.g., correctness or goodness) that is associated with that response.
notes: A numeric reading of what the agent chose, independent of the question asked (e.g. "never" → 0, "always" → 1). It is empty for free-text answers, and equal to `response_description` when the agent entered a number. It is *not* an encoding of the scoring — that is `score`.

.warning `response_numeric` and `score` must both be populated and must never be collapsed into a single column: a reader would then be unable to tell whether the numbers are raw answers, option positions, or already reverse-coded, which can render the dataset unusable.

fields.name: response_time
fields.description: The duration, in seconds, between the earliest possible time a response could have been completed and the moment that response was actually completed (not when it was initiated).

fields.name: response_datetime
fields.description: The datetime corresponding to the completion of the response.

fields.name: response_validation_time
fields.description: In some cases, agents may need to press an extra key to validate previous responses. When relevant, this variable may encode this duration.

fields.name: response_initiation_time
fields.description: In some cases (e.g., a reaching movement) it might be useful to encode when a response was initiated.

fields.name: response_skipped
fields.description: In some cases (e.g., in some questionnaires), agents have the option to skip a question.

fields.name: timed_out
fields.description: Some tasks require agents to give a response within a certain time limit. When agents fail to respond before that time runs out, timed_out is set to TRUE.

fields.name: accuracy
fields.description: A task-dependent accuracy measure ranging from 0 to 1 (inclusive).

fields.name: correct
fields.description: Indicates whether the response matches the expected response (i.e., correct = TRUE) or not (i.e., correct = FALSE).

fields.name: score
fields.description: A numeric value associated with a particular response in a given context. This variable may be used to compute a performance metric or a questionnaire level index (e.g., a well-being score).
notes: For questionnaires, `score` is the value the experimenter assigns to an answer in this particular context. In the BIS/BAS questionnaire, answering "very true for me" yields a score of 1 for some items, 4 for reverse-coded items, and 0 for filler items; item scores are then aggregated into questionnaire-level scores.
.warning `score` and `response_numeric` capture different things and must both be present: `response_numeric` is the raw answer, `score` is its interpretation in this context.

fields.name: evaluation_label
fields.description: There are several labels that can be assigned to a given response to specify what that response means in terms of evaluation within a task. The most general terms are "correct” and "error" (which are already given by the correct variable). There are however more specific sets of terms that may apply in different contexts. For example, in a signal detection task, it is common to use labels from the signal detection theory framework (i.e., “hit”, “miss”, “false alarm”, “correct rejection”). In other contexts, researchers might use terms like “omission” or “commission” errors or even things like “perseveration” error (e.g., in the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test). Note that these terms are not always well defined or exclusive. For example, a “hit” is also a “correct” response and a “false alarm” may be synonymous to “commission error”. Whenever possible use the more specific terms (i.e., always use “hit” rather than “correct” when applicable).

values.description: The response is correct.
The response is incorrect.
The stimulus was *present* and the agent correctly responded *present*.
The stimulus was *present* and the agent incorrectly responded *absent*.
The stimulus was *absent* and the agent incorrectly responded *present* (a false alarm).
The stimulus was *absent* and the agent correctly responded *absent* (a correct rejection).

fields.name: feedback_description
fields.description: Lists the different kinds of feedback that were shown on a given trial. When multiple types of feedback were used, feedback will list them using `;` as a separator. If a given type of feedback was shown multiple times during a trial, that feedback type is listed only once (i.e., feedback_description does *not* represent the sequence of feedbacks).

values.description: No feedback was shown.
Feedback indicated what the correct response would have been.
Feedback explains *why* a certain option is the correct one.
Feedback indicates, on the option itself, whether the option chosen by the participant was the correct one (e.g., in green) or not (e.g., in red).
Feedback displayed at the screen center indicates whether the response to the current trial was correct (e.g., using a green check or a red cross).

notes: This list is not exhaustive and characterizing feedback in the future will involve more variables (e.g., separating the type of information shown (e.g., correctness) and how it is shown (“on_option” versus “on_screen”).
NOTE2: We don’t consider here as “feedback”, the kind of feedback that is used in UI to confirm to users that a button has indeed been clicked.

fields.name: outcome_description
fields.description: Describes the observable consequences of the agent's response (e.g., "the opened box is empty").

fields.name: outcome_numeric
fields.description: A numeric value describing the observable consequences of the agent's response (e.g., +3 points).

fields.name: additional_measures
fields.description: Indicates whether additional measures have been recorded during this trial and, if so, what kind of measures they are.
notes: Leave this field empty if no additional measures were recorded for this specific response.

fields.name: adaptive_method_name
fields.description: Specifies the adaptive procedure used to modify instrument parameters in response to agent performance (e.g., `staircase`).

fields.name: adaptive_method_config
fields.description: More detailed configuration for the adaptive method, including initial values, step sizes, and termination criteria.
notes: For example, `1up-2down`. The 1-up, 2-down is a common adaptive staircase procedure used to estimate an agent's threshold or sensitivity. After a correct response, the difficulty level is increased, and after two incorrect responses, the difficulty level is decreased.

fields.name: adaptive_parameter_name
fields.description: Specific instrument parameter that is dynamically modified based on the agent's performance.

fields.name: adaptive_parameter_value
fields.description: The specific value of the instrument parameter that was used for this trial. This value is updated as the adaptive algorithm adjusts the parameter based on the agent's responses.
fields.range: data type depends on the adaptive parameter, as defined in `adaptive_parameter_name`

fields.name: adaptive_parameter_value_next
fields.description: The next value of the adaptive parameter that will be used in the subsequent trial, as determined by the adaptive algorithm.
fields.range: data type depends on the adaptive parameter, as defined in `adaptive_parameter_name`

tables.name: Stimulus
tables.label: Stimulus
tables.description: Describes each of the stimuli that were shown during a trial.
notes: Each trial can contain a different number of stimuli.

fields.name: runtime_id
fields.description: Identifies the activity run (one specific execution of an activity by one agent, distinguishing restarts) this stimulus belongs to. Unique dataset-wide, so rows stay distinguishable when files from different agents, sessions, or attempts are concatenated. Together with `stimulus_id` it forms this table's dataset-wide key.

fields.name: stimulus_id
fields.description: Primary key of the `Stimulus` table. References to this identifier in other tables are thus named `stimulus_id`.
notes: If the same stimulus is shown at two different times in a trial, those two instances will have their own row in the `Stimulus` table, each with its own `id`.

Make sure to refer to this field as `stimulus_id` rather than `id` When joining tables. This also applies to all the `id` fields; they are named `id` within their own context/table, but `<context/table>_id` when addressed from other tables. For example, `X_id` in a table refers (hence a foreign key) to the `id` column in the X table.

fields.name: trial_index
fields.description: Refers to the `trial_index` in the `Response` table and indicates in which trial this stimulus was shown.
fields.range: `trial_index` in the `Response` table, within the same `runtime_id`

fields.name: response_id
fields.description: Refers to the `response_id` in the `Response` table and indicates for which response this stimulus was shown.
fields.range: `response_id` in the `Response` table, within the same `runtime_id`

fields.name: object_id
fields.description: A stimulus is defined by a set of features. This variable is used to identify each time the same stimulus features were used.
notes: For example, if the same white digit "3" is shown in a digit span sequence, all those instances would have the same `object_id` although they would have different `id`s (as they appeared at different times).

fields.name: presentation_id
fields.description: In a multitasking setting, a particular instance of a stimulus (e.g., the current letter "A") may be used by multiple tasks at the same time (e.g, in the dual N-back task). Because these are different trials, they will have different `trial_index` values and hence will have different rows in the `Stimulus` table. We use `presentation_id` to indicate that a given stimulus is in fact the same instance across those trials.

fields.name: index_in_trial
fields.description: Refers to individual stimuli within the sequence or set of stimuli shown during a trial.

fields.name: onset
fields.description: Duration between the start of the trial and the appearance of the stimulus, in seconds.

fields.name: duration
fields.description: Describes for how long this stimulus was displayed after its onset, in seconds.
notes: When the stimulus is shown using an animation, `duration` covers the complete period between the start of the animation and the end of the animation.

fields.name: panel_id
fields.description: Identifier of the panel this stimulus is displayed over.

fields.name: x_screen
fields.description: X coordinates of the stimulus on the screen in pixels.
notes: In BDM, the preferred position is the center of the object. However, specific implementations of the tasks may use other locations such as the top-left corner. If this is the case, it should be explicitly stated in the [dataset card](https://behaverse.org/data-model/spec/dataset-cards.html).

fields.name: y_screen
fields.description: Y coordinates of the stimulus on the screen in pixels.

fields.name: x_viewport
fields.description: X coordinates of the stimulus on the screen expressed as a fraction of the screen width.

fields.name: y_viewport
fields.description: Y coordinates of the stimulus on the screen expressed as a fraction of the screen height.

fields.name: description
fields.description: A human readable, compact description of the main aspects of the stimulus. The description for a given stimulus depends on the task but follows a specific template for a given task. Because of this, it looks like the `description` could be parsed and converted into a more structured format---however, this is not the intention; structured data will be available in other tables; here, description is for human readability and facilitates the understanding of the data.

fields.name: source
fields.description: Refers to the specific generator or set the stimulus belongs to.
notes: Stimuli that come from the same source have the same data scheme and could thus be described in a table named after the `stimulus_source`. `stimulus_source` indicates which table contains the full information about the stimulus; e.g., "digits1to9".

One could include a `source_count` variable here that indicates how many different stimuli there are in the set; but it's better stored in the table that contains information about that stimulus source.

fields.name: source_type
fields.description: A stimulus is typically created using a particular procedure/algorithm ("generator") or is sampled from a particular set ("set"). This variable indicates which of these two applies for the current stimulus.

values.description: Sampled from a fixed set.
Created using a procedure/algorithm.

fields.name: index_in_source
fields.description: When a stimulus is picked from a particular set (e.g., "digits1to9"), this index refers to the index within that set.
notes: In addition to `index_in_source`, `stimulus_id` can also be used to look up further information about the stimulus in the source.

fields.name: role
fields.description: Describes the role the stimulus plays in the trial.

values.description: A stimulus the agent must process and which should trigger the completion of the response (e.g., classify, reach, memorize) if the agent is doing the task as intended. In some cases (e.g., in a go/no-go task) the correct response to a stimulus is to *not* click the button; the stimulus that triggered the decision not to click the button is still a *target*.
A stimulus the agent must process but which does not trigger the completion of the response (e.g., the first two stimuli in a 2-back test).
A stimulus the agent should not process at all (i.e., ignore) and which is unrelated to the correct execution of the task.
A stimulus giving spatial location information that agents could use to improve their performance.
A stimulus specifying which job the agent should perform.
A stimulus signaling the agent that they should abort the current action.
A stimulus indicating which stimulus to respond about.

fields.name: animation
fields.description: Describes the animation used to display a specific stimulus in a human-readable format. For example, "fadeIn 3s" indicates a 3-second fade-in animation.
notes: To maintain clarity and consistency, BDM recommends using CSS-style naming conventions for common animations (e.g., "3s linear slide-in").

tables.name: Option
tables.label: Option
tables.description: Describes each option that an agent could choose from in a trial.
notes: Note that in some tasks, the options may change within a trial after each input (e.g., serial self-ordered search task); therefore the options are optionally indexed by `input_index`.

fields.name: runtime_id
fields.description: Identifies the activity run (one specific execution of an activity by one agent, distinguishing restarts) this option belongs to. Unique dataset-wide, so rows stay distinguishable when files from different agents, sessions, or attempts are concatenated. Together with `option_id` it forms this table's dataset-wide key.

fields.name: option_id
fields.description: Primary key of the `Option` table. References to this identifier in other tables are thus named `option_id`.
notes: If the same option is shown at two different times in a trial, those two instances will have their own row in the `Option` table, each with its own `id`.

fields.name: trial_index
fields.description: Refers to the `trial_index` in the `Response` table and indicates in which trial this option was shown.
fields.range: `trial_index` in the `Response` table, within the same `runtime_id`

fields.name: response_id
fields.description: Refers to the `response_id` in the `Response` table and indicates for which response this option was shown.
fields.range: `response_id` in the `Response` table, within the same `runtime_id`

fields.name: index_in_trial
fields.description: Indexing each of the options within the set of options that were available to agents on a given trial.
notes: If the presented options have no specific temporal or spatial order, leave this field empty or assign the same index to all options, e.g., `index_in_trial=1`.

fields.name: object_id
fields.description: An option is defined by a set of features. This variable is used to identify each time the same features were used. For example, if the same white digit "3" is used as an option in the Digit Span task, all those instances would have the same `object_id` although they would have different `id`s (as they appeared at different times).

fields.name: onset
fields.description: Duration between the start of the trial and the moment the option was displayed or activated, in seconds.
notes: In questionnaires this is typically 0, since the options usually appear together with the question.

fields.name: duration
fields.description: How long the option was displayed or active in seconds, starting from the `onset`, in seconds.

fields.name: panel_id
fields.description: Identifier of the pane this option was displayed over.

fields.name: x_screen
fields.description: X coordinates of the option component on the screen in pixels.
notes: In BDM, the preferred position is the center of the object. However, specific implementations of the tasks may use other locations such as the top-left corner. If this is the case, it should be explicitly stated in the [dataset card](https://behaverse.org/data-model/spec/dataset-cards.html).

fields.name: y_screen
fields.description: Y coordinates of the option component on the screen in pixels.

fields.name: x_viewport
fields.description: X coordinates of the option component on the screen expressed as a fraction of the screen width.

fields.name: y_viewport
fields.description: Y coordinates of the option component on the screen expressed as a fraction of the screen height.

fields.name: description
fields.description: A human readable, compact description of the main aspects of the option. The description for a given option depends on the task but follows a specific template for a given task. Because of this, it looks like the option description could be parsed---however, this is not the intention; structured, parsed data will be available in other fields; description is for human readability and facilitates the understanding of the data.

fields.name: value
fields.description: A numeric value associated with a particular response option; typically indicating the "worth" of a response (e.g., `value=1` for the correct response).

fields.name: source
fields.description: Refers to the specific generator or set from which the option originates. Options sharing the same source have the same data structure and can be thus collectively described in a table named after `option_source` (e.g., "digit1to9").
notes: The `option_source` specifies the table or file that provides complete details about the option. For instance, `option_source=digit1to9` indicates a source containing information on digits 1 to 9.

fields.name: source_type
fields.description: An option is typically created using a particular procedure/algorithm or is sampled from a particular set. This variable indicates which of these two applies for the current option.

values.description: Sampled from a fixed set.
Created using a procedure/algorithm.

fields.name: index_in_source
fields.description: When an option is picked from a particular set (e.g., `digits1to9`), this index refers to the index within that set.

fields.name: animation
fields.description: Describes the animation used to display a specific option in a human-readable format. For example, "fadeIn 3s ease-in-out" indicates a 3-second fade-in animation.
notes: To maintain clarity and consistency, BDM recommends using CSS-style naming conventions for common animations (e.g., "3s linear slide-in").

tables.name: Input
tables.label: Input
tables.description: A detailed log of all inputs and clicks recorded during the trial.

fields.name: runtime_id
fields.description: Identifies the activity run (one specific execution of an activity by one agent, distinguishing restarts) this input belongs to. Unique dataset-wide, so rows stay distinguishable when files from different agents, sessions, or attempts are concatenated. Together with `input_id` it forms this table's dataset-wide key.

fields.name: input_id
fields.description: Primary key; each input or click has its own identifier value that is unique within the table.

fields.name: response_id
fields.description: Refers to the `response_id` in the `Response` table and indicates for which response this input was recorded.

fields.name: response_element_index
fields.description: Indicates which of the clicks is used and in what order to form the actual response in the response table when `response_structure` is "sequence" or "set".
fields.range: 1 to `input_count` in the corresponding row of the `Response` table
notes: This needs to be here rather than in `Option` table, because the same option can be clicked multiple times and either serve or not for the response depending on the order of the clicks. For example, in the Digit Span test we could have the response of "3;5;7" on a particular trial. This might correspond to > - `option.description` = ["3", "4", "delete", "delete", "3", "5", "7", "enter"] > - `click.response_element_index` = [NA, NA, NA, NA, 1, 2, 3, NA]

fields.name: onset
fields.description: Duration between the start of the trial and the moment the mouse button press occurred, in seconds.

fields.name: duration
fields.description: Describes for how long the mouse button was pressed, in seconds.

fields.name: x_screen
fields.description: X coordinates of the click relative to the left edge of the screen in pixels.

fields.name: y_screen
fields.description: Y coordinates of the click relative to the top edge of the screen in pixels.

fields.name: x_viewport
fields.description: X coordinates of the click relative to the left edge of the screen expressed as a fraction of the screen width.

fields.name: y_viewport
fields.description: Y coordinates of the click relative to the top edge of the screen expressed as a fraction of the screen height.

fields.name: object_type
fields.description: Describes the type of object that was clicked on (e.g., "button").

fields.name: object_name
fields.description: The human-readable name of the object that was clicked on (e.g., "sos_box_1_3").

fields.name: is_object_enabled
fields.description: Indicates whether the object that was clicked on was enabled (clickable) or not.

fields.name: object_state
fields.description: Describes the state the object was in *before* it was clicked on. The meaning of "state" depends on the particular task (e.g., "new empty").

fields.name: option_id
fields.description: If the click is on an option, this variable indicates which option it was.
fields.range: `option_id` in the `Option` table, within the same `runtime_id`

fields.name: stimulus_id
fields.description: If the click is on a stimulus, this variable indicates which stimulus it was.
fields.range: `stimulus_id` in the `Stimulus` table, within the same `runtime_id`

tables.name: StimulusComponent
tables.label: StimulusComponent
tables.description: Stimuli can comprise multiple components. This table describes each component of a stimulus.

fields.name: runtime_id
fields.description: Identifies the activity run (one specific execution of an activity by one agent, distinguishing restarts) this stimulus component belongs to. Unique dataset-wide, so rows stay distinguishable when files from different agents, sessions, or attempts are concatenated. Together with (`stimulus_id`, `index`) it forms this table's dataset-wide key.

fields.name: stimulus_id
fields.description: A reference to the primary key `stimulus_id` of the `Stimulus` table.
fields.range: `stimulus_id` in the `Stimulus` table, within the same `runtime_id`

fields.name: index
fields.description: A 1-based index indicating the stacking order of stimulus components. A stimulus component with a higher `index` is displayed on top of those with lower values, similar to CSS z-index property.
notes: If the presented options have no specific temporal or spatial order, leave this field empty or assign the same index to all options, e.g., `index=1`.

fields.name: x_screen
fields.description: X coordinates of the stimulus component relative to the left edge of the screen in pixels.
notes: In BDM, the preferred position is the center of the object. However, specific implementations of the tasks may use other locations such as the top-left corner. If this is the case, it should be explicitly stated in the [dataset card](https://behaverse.org/data-model/spec/dataset-cards.html).

fields.name: y_screen
fields.description: Y coordinates of the stimulus component relative to the top edge of the screen in pixels.

fields.name: x_viewport
fields.description: X coordinates of the stimulus component relative to the left edge of the screen expressed as a fraction of the screen width.

fields.name: y_viewport
fields.description: Y coordinates of the stimulus component relative to the top edge of the screen expressed as a fraction of the screen height.

fields.name: description
fields.description: A human readable, compact description of the component.

fields.name: symbol_name
fields.description: The human-readable name of the displayed symbol.

fields.name: symbol_count
fields.description: The number of symbols represented in this component.

fields.name: symbol_layout
fields.description: How the symbols are laid out.

values.description: Along the Y axis.
Along the X axis.

notes: If none of the predefined layouts apply, leave this field empty or use a custom human-readable label. Make sure custom labels are clearly defined in the codebook.

fields.name: color_name
fields.description: The human-readable name of the component color, e.g., `red`.
notes: To maintain clarity and consistency, BDM recommends using CSS-style naming conventions for colors (e.g., "lightgray").

fields.name: color_hex
fields.description: The hexadecimal RGB color code of the component (e.g., #FF0000 for red) with optional alpha channel for transparency.

fields.name: orientation
fields.description: Indicates the symbol orientation.

values.description: Bottom to top.
Left to right.
Top to bottom.
Right to left.
No specific orientation.

notes: If none of the predefined orientations apply, leave this field empty or use a custom human-readable label. Make sure custom labels are clearly defined in the codebook.

tables.name: OptionComponent
tables.label: OptionComponent
tables.description: Options can comprise multiple components. This table describes each component of an option.

fields.name: runtime_id
fields.description: Identifies the activity run (one specific execution of an activity by one agent, distinguishing restarts) this option component belongs to. Unique dataset-wide, so rows stay distinguishable when files from different agents, sessions, or attempts are concatenated. Together with (`option_id`, `index`) it forms this table's dataset-wide key.

fields.name: index
fields.description: A 1-based index differentiating each part and indicating the stacking order of them. An option component with a higher `index` is displayed on top of those with lower values, similar to CSS z-index property.

fields.name: option_id
fields.description: A reference to the key `option_id` in the `Option` table.
fields.range: `option_id` in the `Option` table, within the same `runtime_id`

fields.name: panel_id
fields.description: Identifier of the panel this option is displayed over.

fields.name: x_screen
fields.description: X coordinates of the option component relative to the left edge of the screen in pixels.
notes: In BDM, the preferred position is the center of the object. However, specific implementations of the tasks may use other locations such as the top-left corner. If this is the case, it should be explicitly stated in the [dataset card](https://behaverse.org/data-model/spec/dataset-cards.html).

fields.name: y_screen
fields.description: Y coordinates of the option component relative to the top edge of the screen in pixels.

fields.name: x_viewport
fields.description: X coordinates of the option component relative to the left edge of the screen expressed as a fraction of the screen width.

fields.name: y_viewport
fields.description: Y coordinates of the option component relative to the top edge of the screen expressed as a fraction of the screen height.

fields.name: description
fields.description: A human readable, compact description of the component.

fields.name: symbol_name
fields.description: The name of the displayed symbol.

fields.name: symbol_count
fields.description: The number of symbols represented in this component.

fields.name: symbol_layout
fields.description: How the symbols are laid out.

values.description: Along the Y axis.
Along the X axis.

notes: If none of the predefined layouts apply, leave this field empty or use a custom human-readable label. Make sure custom labels are clearly defined in the codebook.

fields.name: color_name
fields.description: The human-readable name of the component color, e.g., `red`.
notes: To maintain clarity and consistency, BDM recommends using CSS-style naming conventions for colors (e.g., "lightgray").

fields.name: color_hex
fields.description: The hexadecimal RGB color code of the component (e.g., #FF0000 for red) with optional alpha channel for transparency.

fields.name: orientation
fields.description: Indicates the symbol orientation.

values.description: Bottom to top.
Left to right.
Top to bottom.
Right to left.
No specific orientation.

notes: If none of the predefined orientations apply, leave this field empty or use a custom human-readable label. Make sure custom labels are clearly defined in the codebook.

tables.name: Instrument
tables.label: Instrument
tables.description: Describes the instrument used for data acquisition.
notes: A row describes a specific parameterization of an instrument (a timeline) — for example, the parameters of the software that presents the stimuli and records the key presses.

fields.name: instrument_id
fields.description: Unique identifier of an instrument. It can be formed by combining name and version (e.g., "DS_v2024.01").

fields.name: timeline_id
fields.description: Identifier for a timeline. Timeline is a variant of an instrument with specific parameterization, for the whole experiment or for multiple block of trials (e.g., "DS_FORWARD" and "DS_BACKWARD" for digit span task). Timelines are configurations that specify instrument parameters.

fields.name: block_id
fields.description: Specific parameterization of the instrument for a single block of trials (e.g., "DS_FORWARD_PRACTICE" and "DS_FORWARD_TEST"). Block-level parameters override timeline-level parameters.

fields.name: name
fields.description: Name of the toolkit (scene, code, or configuration) that is used to collect the data, e.g., "DS" for a software that runs digit span task in forward or backward order. The specific parameterization of the instrument is defined by the "Timeline" (e.g., a variant of instrument called "DS_FORWARD").

fields.name: version
fields.description: Refers to the specific version/build of a particular instrument. We will use a calendar based versioning system ([calver.org](https://calver.org/); e.g., "v2024.01").

fields.name: description
fields.description: A human readable, compact description of the main aspects of the instrument.

fields.name: link
fields.description: External link, if any, the provides more information about the instrument, e.g., on Cognitive Atlas.
notes: Permanent links, e.g., DOIs, are preferred over particular websites.

tables.name: Subtrial
tables.label: Subtrial
tables.description: Per-stage detail for trials composed of successive, dependent stages, each with its own stimulus → response → outcome cycle (e.g., the two-step task). The trial row in `Response` remains *the* unit and carries the trial-level (aggregate or final) response and evaluation; each `Subtrial` row is a miniature trial anatomy for one stage.
notes: Simple single-stage trials need no rows here (`subtrial_count` = 1 in the `Response` table).
The stage count of a trial is derived: `subtrial_count` = max `subtrial_index` among the trial's rows.

Do not confuse stages with the pieces of one response: a digit-span trial recalling "3-5-7" is *one* subtrial with `response_count` = 3 in the `Response` table; a two-step trial is *two* subtrials, each with its own stimulus and outcome.

fields.name: runtime_id
fields.description: Identifies the activity run (one specific execution of an activity by one agent, distinguishing restarts) this subtrial belongs to. Unique dataset-wide, so rows stay distinguishable when files from different agents, sessions, or attempts are concatenated. Together with `subtrial_id` it forms this table's dataset-wide key.

fields.name: subtrial_id
fields.description: Primary key; each subtrial row has its own identifier, unique within the table.

fields.name: trial_index
fields.description: Refers to the `trial_index` in the `Response` table and indicates which trial this stage belongs to.
fields.range: `trial_index` in the `Response` table, within the same `runtime_id`

fields.name: response_id
fields.description: Refers to the `response_id` in the `Response` table for the parent trial's response row.
fields.range: `response_id` in the `Response` table, within the same `runtime_id`

fields.name: subtrial_index
fields.description: The 1-based order of this stage within its trial (i.e., the first stage of a trial has `subtrial_index` = 1).
fields.range: 1-based index of the stage within the trial

fields.name: task_index
fields.description: When `multitask_type` is not empty, refers to the individual task this stage belongs to, so the same mechanism serves compound and concurrent multitasking. See `task_index` in the `Response` table.

fields.name: onset
fields.description: Duration between the start of the trial and the start of this stage, in seconds.

fields.name: duration
fields.description: How long this stage lasted, from its onset, in seconds.

fields.name: stimulus_id
fields.description: The stimulus (or stimulus set/sequence) presented in this stage.
fields.range: `stimulus_id` in the `Stimulus` table, within the same `runtime_id`

fields.name: expected_response_option_index
fields.description: The index of the option the agent is expected to choose in this stage. Same conventions as the `Response` table's field of the same name.

fields.name: response_option_index
fields.description: The index of the option the agent chose in this stage, starting from 1; 0 means none of the options was chosen. Same conventions as the `Response` table's field of the same name.

fields.name: response_description
fields.description: A description of the agent's response in this stage; typically the description of the chosen option.

fields.name: response_numeric
fields.description: A numeric value associated with this stage's response (e.g., a typed number or the numeric meaning of the selected option).

fields.name: response_time
fields.description: The duration, in seconds, between the earliest possible time this stage's response could have been completed and the moment it was actually completed.

fields.name: correct
fields.description: Whether this stage's response matches the expected response.

fields.name: accuracy
fields.description: A task-dependent accuracy measure for this stage, ranging from 0 to 1 (inclusive).

fields.name: score
fields.description: A numeric value associated with this stage's response in a given context.

fields.name: evaluation_label
fields.description: Evaluation label for this stage's response (e.g., `correct`, `error`, `hit`, `miss`). Same conventions as the `Response` table's field of the same name.

values.description: The response is correct.
The response is incorrect.
The stimulus was *present* and the agent correctly responded *present*.
The stimulus was *present* and the agent incorrectly responded *absent*.
The stimulus was *absent* and the agent incorrectly responded *present* (a false alarm).
The stimulus was *absent* and the agent correctly responded *absent* (a correct rejection).

fields.name: outcome_description
fields.description: The observable consequence of this stage's response (e.g., the two-step's stage-1 transition, or stage-2 reward).

fields.name: outcome_numeric
fields.description: A numeric value describing the observable consequence of this stage's response (e.g., +3 points).

tables.name: TrialParameter
tables.label: TrialParameter
tables.description: Per-trial (and per-subtrial) ground-truth *generative* task parameters — latent task state, not behavior — in long format: one row per parameter, per grid cell, per trial. These are the values that vary from trial to trial within a run, such as a two-step task's drifting reward probabilities. Serves simulation, parameter recovery, and engine calibration.
notes: The natural key is (`runtime_id`, `response_id`, `subtrial_index`, `task_index`, `parameter`, `parameter_index`).
Values that are constant across a whole activity run belong in the `TaskParameter` table instead; joining the two on `runtime_id` reconstructs the full generative state in effect on any trial.

These values are legitimate inputs for simulation and recovery tooling, but they are *not* legitimate predictors for models of behavior: analysis pipelines should refuse (or loudly flag) any model that consumes ground-truth task parameters when predicting the very responses those parameters generated.

fields.name: runtime_id
fields.description: Identifies the activity run this row's trial belongs to. Unique dataset-wide, so rows stay distinguishable when files are concatenated.

fields.name: response_id
fields.description: Refers to the `response_id` in the `Response` table: the trial whose generative state this row records.
fields.range: `response_id` in the `Response` table, within the same `runtime_id`

fields.name: trial_index
fields.description: Refers to the `trial_index` in the `Response` table for the same trial. Redundant with `response_id`; kept because the sibling detail tables carry both.
fields.range: `trial_index` in the `Response` table, within the same `runtime_id`

fields.name: subtrial_index
fields.description: When the parameter is realized at a specific stage of a staged trial, the 1-based `subtrial_index` of that stage (see the `Subtrial` table). Empty for trial-level parameters.

fields.name: task_index
fields.description: When `multitask_type` is not empty, the individual task this parameter belongs to.

fields.name: parameter
fields.description: Name of the generative parameter (e.g., `p_reward`, `slot_mean`, `drift_rate`). What the parameter means, its unit, and the meaning of its dimensions belong in the dataset's codebook.

fields.name: parameter_dimensions
fields.description: Names of the parameter's coordinate axes, in order — e.g. `state;action` for a per-(state, action) reward probability. Empty for scalar parameters. Repeating the names on every row keeps the file readable without a codebook lookup.
notes: Use semicolon-separated names on CSV export, e.g. `state;action`.

fields.name: parameter_index
fields.description: This row's coordinates within the parameter's index space, in the same order as `parameter_dimensions` — e.g. `1;2` means state 1, action 2. Empty for scalar parameters. There is no fixed limit on the number of dimensions, so grids of any arity (including a transition tensor indexed by state, action, and next state) are expressible.
notes: Use semicolon-separated indices on CSV export, e.g. `1;2`.
A vector-valued parameter is represented as one row per element, with the element position carried here — that is the tidy form, and the reason parameters are not packed into wide columns.

fields.name: value_numeric
fields.description: The parameter's value when it is numeric. Mirrors the `*_numeric` / `*_description` pairing used for responses and outcomes, so each column keeps a usable type instead of collapsing to a mixed-type column.

fields.name: value_description
fields.description: The parameter's value when it is textual or categorical (e.g. a named reward schedule), or a human-readable rendering of a numeric value.

tables.name: TaskParameter
tables.label: TaskParameter
tables.description: Per-activity-run ground-truth *generative* task parameters — latent task state, not behavior — in long format: one row per parameter and grid cell per run. These are the values that stay constant across one run of an activity but vary between runs and agents, such as a per-agent fixed reward mapping or a per-group volatility level.
notes: The natural key is (`runtime_id`, `task_index`, `parameter`, `parameter_index`). The grain is the activity run, so there is no `response_id` — the value applies to all of the run's trials.
Values that change from trial to trial belong in the `TrialParameter` table instead; joining the two on `runtime_id` reconstructs the full generative state in effect on any trial.
The instrument-level configuration that generated these values (drift hyperparameters, fixed task constants) is a different level of description and is not represented here.
The `TrialParameter` rule applies here too: ground-truth parameters are inputs for simulation and recovery tooling, never predictors of the responses they generated.

fields.name: runtime_id
fields.description: Identifies the activity run these parameters describe. Unique dataset-wide, so rows stay distinguishable when files are concatenated.

fields.name: agent_id
fields.description: The agent whose run these parameters describe. Carried directly so the file can be read without resolving `runtime_id`.

fields.name: session_index
fields.description: The 1-based session, within the agent, that this run belongs to.

fields.name: instrument_id
fields.description: The instrument (task) these parameters belong to — this is what names the activity the row is about.

fields.name: task_index
fields.description: When `multitask_type` is not empty, the individual task this parameter belongs to.

fields.name: parameter
fields.description: Name of the generative parameter (e.g., `p_reward`, `slot_mean`, `drift_rate`). What the parameter means, its unit, and the meaning of its dimensions belong in the dataset's codebook.

fields.name: parameter_dimensions
fields.description: Names of the parameter's coordinate axes, in order — e.g. `state;action` for a per-(state, action) reward probability. Empty for scalar parameters. Repeating the names on every row keeps the file readable without a codebook lookup.
notes: Use semicolon-separated names on CSV export, e.g. `state;action`.

fields.name: parameter_index
fields.description: This row's coordinates within the parameter's index space, in the same order as `parameter_dimensions` — e.g. `1;2` means state 1, action 2. Empty for scalar parameters. There is no fixed limit on the number of dimensions, so grids of any arity (including a transition tensor indexed by state, action, and next state) are expressible.
notes: Use semicolon-separated indices on CSV export, e.g. `1;2`.
A vector-valued parameter is represented as one row per element, with the element position carried here — that is the tidy form, and the reason parameters are not packed into wide columns.

fields.name: value_numeric
fields.description: The parameter's value when it is numeric. Mirrors the `*_numeric` / `*_description` pairing used for responses and outcomes, so each column keeps a usable type instead of collapsing to a mixed-type column.

fields.name: value_description
fields.description: The parameter's value when it is textual or categorical (e.g. a named reward schedule), or a human-readable rendering of a numeric value.

tables.name: Score
tables.label: Score
tables.description: Scores summarizing a whole activity run — a questionnaire subscale total, a span threshold, a d-prime, a staircase estimate. Long format: one row per score, so a single scoring method that produces several scores writes several rows. These are *derived* values, computed from the trial tables (or, for fitted estimates, by the instrument itself); they are not raw measurements.
notes: The natural key is (`runtime_id`, `score_name`, `score_index`).

Scope is *one* activity run: both `runtime_id` and `instrument_id` are required. A score spanning several runs or several instruments within a session — a battery-wide index, a cross-test composite — is deliberately not expressible here. Such a score has a different grain, and mixing grains in one table is exactly what the `TrialParameter`/`TaskParameter` split exists to avoid; if a concrete case arises it warrants its own table rather than optional scope keys here.
Trial-level evaluation stays in the `Response` table (`accuracy`, `score`, `evaluation_label`). This table is one level up: it summarizes the run, not a single response.

Some scores *cannot* be recomputed from the trial tables — an adaptive threshold is produced by the estimator built into the instrument, not by a formula over the recorded trials. Recording them here is what makes those datasets reusable.

`method` records how a value was produced and `classification` where that value falls against a stated reference; a classification without its `classification_reference` is uninterpretable, because two datasets applying different cutoffs would look identical.

fields.name: runtime_id
fields.description: Identifies the activity run this score summarizes. Unique dataset-wide, so rows stay distinguishable when files are concatenated.

fields.name: agent_id
fields.description: The agent whose run this score summarizes. Carried directly so the file can be read without resolving `runtime_id`.

fields.name: session_index
fields.description: The 1-based session, within the agent, that this run belongs to.

fields.name: instrument_id
fields.description: The instrument (task) that was scored.

fields.name: score_name
fields.description: Which score this row holds (e.g. `bis`, `bas_drive`, `span`, `accuracy`). One scoring method may emit several named scores; each gets its own row.

fields.name: score_dimensions
fields.description: Names of the score's coordinate axes, in order — e.g. `block` for a per-block score. Empty for a single score over the whole run.
notes: Use semicolon-separated names on CSV export, e.g. `block;condition`. Same mechanism as `parameter_dimensions` in the parameter tables.

fields.name: score_index
fields.description: This row's coordinates, in the same order as `score_dimensions` — e.g. `2` for the second block. Lets a score be reported per block or per condition without mangling the name (`accuracy_block2`).
notes: Use semicolon-separated indices on CSV export, e.g. `1;2`.

fields.name: score_numeric
fields.description: The score, when it is numeric.

fields.name: score_description
fields.description: The score, when it is textual or categorical (e.g. a screening outcome of `positive`), or a human-readable rendering of a numeric score.

fields.name: method
fields.description: How the score was produced: a summary operation (`sum`, `mean`, `proportion_correct`), a derived measure (`d_prime`), or a named estimator (`staircase_threshold`). Without it a number is uninterpretable — a raw total and a fitted estimate look identical.

fields.name: method_version
fields.description: Version or parameterization of the scoring method, where the recipe can vary (e.g. `1up-2down` for a staircase, or a version tag for a revised scoring key).

fields.name: classification
fields.description: The band this score falls into when compared against a stated reference (e.g. `below_average`, `clinical`, `underweight`). Distinct from the score itself: the value is what was measured, the classification is where it falls.

fields.name: classification_reference
fields.description: The norms, cutoffs, or published criteria the `classification` came from (e.g. `Carver & White (1994)`). Required in practice whenever `classification` is set: without it the band cannot be reproduced or compared across datasets.

fields.name: unit
fields.description: Unit of the numeric score where one applies (e.g. `items`, `ms`, `proportion`). Omit for unitless scores.
